content: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent and systemic inflammation of the synovial lining of joints and tendon sheaths. Currently, there is no definitive cure for this condition. Treatment strategies primarily focus on symptom management, including alleviation of pain, reduction of stiffness, and improvement of mobility, with the ultimate goal of achieving stable remission and enhancing the patient’s quality of life. Celecoxib, a selective cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitor, is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) commonly used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of celecoxib in individuals with rheumatoid arthritis. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and clinical trial registries, up to May 18, 2017. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing oral celecoxib (200 mg or 400 mg daily) to placebo, no intervention, or traditional NSAIDs (tNSAIDs) were included. Studies with fewer than 50 participants per arm or treatment durations of less than four weeks were excluded. Eight RCTs, published between 1998 and 2014, were included in the analysis, involving a total of 3,988 adult participants (mean age 54 years, 73% female) with an average disease duration of 9.2 years. The studies were assessed as having a high or unclear risk of bias in at least one domain, and the overall quality of evidence was rated as moderate to low. Five of the studies were funded by pharmaceutical companies. Celecoxib versus Placebo Two studies (873 participants) compared celecoxib (200 mg or 400 mg daily) to placebo. Participants receiving celecoxib demonstrated significant clinical improvement compared to those on placebo, with a 15% absolute improvement (relative risk [RR] 1.53, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.25 to 1.86). The number needed to treat to benefit (NNTB) was 7 (95% CI 5 to 13). Celecoxib also resulted in an 11% absolute reduction in pain compared to placebo (NNTB = 4, 95% CI 3 to 6). However, the evidence for improvement in physical function was inconclusive (mean difference [MD] -0.10, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.10). In terms of adverse events, 15 out of 293 participants in the celecoxib group developed ulcers, compared to 4 out of 99 in the placebo group (Peto odds ratio [OR] 1.26, 95% CI 0.44 to 3.63). Serious adverse events were reported in 9 out of 475 participants in the celecoxib group and 5 out of 231 in the placebo group (Peto OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.28 to 2.69). Withdrawals were less frequent in the celecoxib group (22% absolute reduction, RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.72). Cardiovascular events, such as myocardial infarction or stroke, were not reported in these studies, but regulatory agencies have previously warned of an increased cardiovascular risk associated with celecoxib. Celecoxib versus Traditional NSAIDs Seven studies (2,930 participants) compared celecoxib to tNSAIDs, including amtolmetin guacyl, diclofenac, ibuprofen, meloxicam, nabumetone, naproxen, and pelubiprofen. Celecoxib showed a small improvement in the proportion of participants achieving an ACR20 response (4% absolute improvement, RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.23), but this difference may not be clinically significant. There was no clear evidence of a difference between celecoxib and tNSAIDs in terms of pain reduction or physical function improvement. Participants taking celecoxib had a lower incidence of gastroduodenal ulcers ≥ 3 mm (34 out of 870) compared to those on tNSAIDs (116 out of 698), corresponding to a 12% absolute reduction (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.32). Withdrawals were also less frequent in the celecoxib group (7% absolute reduction, RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.86). Serious adverse events were reported in 17 out of 918 participants in the celecoxib group and 42 out of 1,236 in the tNSAID group (Peto OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.28). Cardiovascular events were reported in both groups in one study involving 149 participants, but the results were inconclusive. Authors' Conclusions Celecoxib may provide clinical benefits, including symptom improvement and pain relief, compared to placebo, but its effect on physical function remains uncertain. Compared to tNSAIDs, celecoxib may slightly improve clinical symptoms and is associated with a lower incidence of gastroduodenal ulcers. However, the evidence for pain reduction, physical function improvement, and cardiovascular safety is inconclusive. The uncertainty surrounding cardiovascular risks may be attributed to the small size and short duration of the included trials. Both celecoxib and tNSAIDs have been previously associated with increased cardiovascular event rates. Larger, long-term head-to-head trials are needed to provide more definitive evidence and guide clinical decision-making.
